_meta.name: Illness & medication growth-interference reference
_meta.note: Powers the Development interference log. Common childhood illnesses with typical durations + the growth mechanism, and medications classified by growth-interference risk. Parent-friendly wording deliberately avoids alarm: the point is that PROLONGED / frequent / high-dose exposure matters, not a single short course. Citations only where web-verified, matching the project's no-fabrication rule.
_meta.risk_tiers: high = documented growth-velocity suppression with prolonged/frequent use; moderate = plausible slowing (usually via appetite) or small effect; neutral = no direct hormonal growth effect.

illnesses.label: Fever (unspecified)
illnesses.growthNote: Fever raises the body's energy demand and usually dips appetite for a few days. Brief episodes rarely touch the growth curve; it's repeated or prolonged fevers that are worth watching.

illnesses.label: Cold / upper respiratory
illnesses.growthNote: A common cold is mild for growth — some appetite drop, quick recovery. No lasting effect on height in a well-nourished child.

illnesses.label: Influenza (flu)
illnesses.growthNote: High metabolic demand — fever burns extra calories — combined with poor appetite. A single bout is temporary; frequent flu seasons with poor intake can show as a brief weight dip.

illnesses.label: RSV / bronchiolitis
illnesses.growthNote: The extra effort of breathing plus poor feeding, especially in infants, can cause a short weight drop. Weight usually recovers once breathing eases.

illnesses.label: COVID-19
illnesses.growthNote: Variable — often mild in children, with an appetite and energy dip. Watch intake during the illness; effect on growth is usually short-lived.

illnesses.label: Gastroenteritis (diarrhea/vomiting)
illnesses.growthNote: The biggest acute growth risk on this list: diarrhea and vomiting cause nutrient malabsorption and real weight loss, and moderate-to-severe or repeated episodes can briefly stall height velocity too. Rehydration and rebuilding intake afterward matter.

illnesses.label: Hand, foot & mouth (HFMD)
illnesses.growthNote: Painful mouth sores lead children to refuse food and fluids, causing a rapid short-term weight drop. Soft, cool foods and hydration through the sore-throat days limit the dip.

illnesses.label: Strep throat
illnesses.growthNote: Painful swallowing restricts calorie intake for a few days. With antibiotics it resolves quickly and intake — and weight — bounce back.

illnesses.label: Asthma flare-up
illnesses.growthNote: The flare itself is short, but recurrent flares mean systemic inflammation and reliance on steroids — so the medication log below matters as much as the illness itself for growth.

illnesses.label: Ear infection
illnesses.growthNote: Pain and disrupted sleep can dampen appetite briefly. Minor for growth on its own; frequent recurrences are worth mentioning to a doctor.

illnesses.label: Skin / rash
illnesses.growthNote: Most rashes have no growth effect. The exception is when a rash is treated with prolonged systemic steroids — track that in the medication log.

illnesses.label: Injury
illnesses.growthNote: Most injuries don't affect growth. A growth-plate (physeal) fracture is the exception and needs orthopedic follow-up, since it can affect the length of that specific bone.

illnesses.label: Hospitalization
illnesses.growthNote: A hospital stay usually signals a more significant illness — the acute stress, reduced intake, and any medications together can produce a visible growth pause. Careful height tracking over the following 1–2 months shows whether catch-up is happening.

illnesses.label: Other
illnesses.growthNote: Log the dates and any medications given. If growth stalls around this period on the chart, it's useful context for your pediatrician.

medications.name: Oral steroid (Prednisolone / Prednisone)
medications.insight: Systemic steroids are the medication class most clearly linked to slowed growth — they lower growth hormone and IGF-1 and slow the growth plates directly. The key nuance: a single short burst (under ~2 weeks) is generally low-risk. The concern is prolonged use (more than a few weeks), high doses, or many repeated short courses. If your child has had a longer or repeated course, log height carefully over the next 1–2 months.
medications.citation: PubMed — PMID/ID: 17675727 — "Minimizing side effects of systemic corticosteroids in children" — Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol — 2007

medications.name: Dexamethasone / Betamethasone
medications.insight: These are much stronger than prednisolone at suppressing growth — roughly 18 times the potency for the same effect — so even shorter courses deserve attention if they're repeated (for example, frequent croup or asthma treatment). Not a reason to skip a needed dose; a reason to track height and discuss frequency with your doctor.
medications.citation: PubMed — PMID/ID: 17675727 — "Minimizing side effects of systemic corticosteroids in children" — Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol — 2007

medications.name: Inhaled steroid (Fluticasone / Budesonide)
medications.insight: Daily inhaled steroids for asthma are largely safe and far lower-dose to the body than oral steroids. Long-term use is linked to a small reduction in adult height — on the order of 1 cm — which is non-progressive and generally outweighed by keeping the asthma controlled. Worth tracking, not worth stopping over.
medications.citation: PMC — PMID/ID: PMC3517799 — "Effect of Inhaled Glucocorticoids in Childhood on Adult Height" — N Engl J Med — 2012

medications.name: ADHD stimulant (Methylphenidate / Amphetamine)
medications.insight: Stimulants suppress appetite, so months-to-years of use can lower weight and then secondarily slow height velocity. The effect is dose-related and largely happens during treatment; final adult height appears little affected for most children. Taking the dose with meals, protein-rich snacks when appetite returns, and watching the growth chart usually let treatment continue safely.
medications.citation: PMC — PMID/ID: PMC9627528 — "Effect of stimulants on final adult height" — 2022

medications.name: Antibiotic (Amoxicillin / Azithromycin)
medications.insight: Antibiotics don't act on growth hormones, so a course to treat an infection is growth-neutral. The only indirect consideration is that very frequent courses can temporarily disturb the gut microbiome and nutrient absorption — so they're useful to track for the pattern, not because a single course affects height.

medications.name: Other medication
medications.insight: Logged for your records. If a medication is taken for many weeks and growth slows around the same period on the chart, that timing is useful information for your pediatrician.
